name: Concurrent Input Mechanisms
explanation: A page shouldn't arbitrarily restrict which input method a user is allowed to use, such as forcing touch-only interaction on a device that also supports a mouse, keyboard, or stylus, or disabling keyboard input just because a touch event was detected recently. Users should be free to switch between whatever input methods their platform supports and even use more than one at once, like typing with a keyboard while also using a touchpad, unless restricting a particular input is essential to the function or necessary for security, such as requiring a physical key press for a security-sensitive confirmation.
whoItAffects: People often rely on more than one input method depending on the task, their physical state that day, or what's convenient in the moment, such as switching between a stylus and a finger on a tablet, or using a mouse for precise pointing and a keyboard for text entry within the same session. People with fluctuating or situational disabities, such as a temporary hand injury, may need to switch input methods on the fly, and rigid restrictions locking them into one input type only can turn a minor inconvenience into a hard barrier.
howToTest: On a device that supports multiple input methods, such as a touchscreen laptop with a keyboard, trackpad, and touch input all available, try switching between them mid-task. Start an interaction with touch, then continue it with the keyboard or mouse, and vice versa. If using one input method disables or breaks the others, or if the page locks you into a single input mode after detecting your first interaction, this fails, unless that restriction is essential or security-related.

check.question: A web app running on a touchscreen laptop detects the first touch interaction and then disables all mouse and keyboard event handlers for the remainder of the session, forcing the user to continue with touch only. Does this pass SC 2.5.6 Concurrent Input Mechanisms?
choices: Yes, because committing to one input type simplifies the interface logic
No, because the page restricts available input modalities without an essential or security-related reason
Yes, because touchscreen laptops are expected to be used with touch primarily
It depends only on whether a setting exists to switch back manually
